# Committing and pushing

**scratch**
: Files and folders that your work makes and `main` does not keep: logs, captured and raw run output, copies of tools, lists and private caches folders.

Your brief says whether you commit and push, and on which branch. If it says nothing, commit on your current branch, and push it.

## What to commit

- Commit your change, its tests, your report if it is a file, and any reusable script.
- Commit what you write to the record, such as a ledger row, with the work that it records. A row's close follows the fix's commit (`records.md`).
- A probe is a task of a brief that builds a change to answer a question and does not land it. Commit its change as a patch file, with its report and programs, in the `probes/` folder that the brief names, and no edit of the original tree. If the brief names no folder, commit nothing of the probe: give the patch's path and the report in your final message.
- Keep scratch in your tree's `tmp/`, which is gitignored.
- Do not commit `.claude/worktrees/` or `.claude/agents/`, which show as untracked in a fresh clone.
- Keep a copyrighted PDF or deck in `research/decks/`, also gitignored. Cite it by its Wayback URL. Notes on it go in `research/extracts/`: your own summary, with brief attributed quotations.
- Put provenance and rationale in commit messages and reports, not in source comments.
- Name a model by its tier (Opus, Sonnet, Fable) in any text that you commit, commit messages included. Never write its model identifier, the API's name for the model, which starts with `claude-`.

## How to commit

Commit as you go, each commit in one command that names its paths:

    git add -- <paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <paths>

- The command commits only the paths that it names. Other agents may have uncommitted edits in your tree. Leave them alone.
- If you renamed a file with `git mv`, name its old path in `git commit` only, because `git add` refuses a path that no longer exists: `git add -- <new paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <new paths> <old paths>`.
- Never commit a copied directory, and never use `git add -A`.
- Before you commit more than a few hundred lines, stage them and read what you staged: `git add -- <paths> && git diff --cached --stat -- <paths>`.
- If the commit edits the original tree, say so in its message.
- End every commit message with this footer, exactly, whatever footer Claude Code suggests:

      Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
      Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01AmiXNpJxQ6TBwec4vJZHDB

  If your brief gives another session line, use it. If a commit that is already made has a footer that names a model, by any name or identifier, leave the commit as it is. Such a footer is not a defect: do not check for it, report it or list it.

## Pushing

Push after every commit.

- If you work on your own branch, push it: `git push -u origin <branch>` the first time, then `git push`. Your brief says how the branch reaches `main`.
- From a session in a cloud container, do not try to delete a branch on GitHub, or retry a refusal with another tool (the `cloud-container` skill, "Rules for every agent"). Removing a worktree leaves its branch. Ask nobody in your report to delete a branch.
- If you work on `main`, other agents commit to it too. Push only your own commits:
  1. Run `git log origin/main..main`. Your commits are those whose hashes your own `git commit` printed.
  2. If it lists another agent's commit, run the command again shortly: that agent pushes right after it commits. If the commit stays, push nothing, and say so in your report.
  3. If it lists only your commits, push the three refs with this one command, and wait for it to end:

         git push --atomic origin main main:claude/worker-brief-fable-vnnuv8 main:blinded-fable

     With `--atomic`, the three refs update together or not at all. Do not pipe the command into another command, since a pipe hides a refusal. A refusal shows as a line that starts with `!`, and as a non-zero exit. The platform rebuilds a lost container from `blinded-fable`.
- Push no branch that this section does not name, unless your brief names it.
- If a push is refused, push nothing more, and do not run it again. Report the refused ref and git's message.

# Running tests

**track**
: One of the four JVMs of `ant testFast`.

**shard**
: One of the four JVMs of `ant testSystem`. Shard i of n takes every n-th file of the sorted list, from index i.

**code state**
: Code of a tree as one edit leaves it. Only an edit of code makes a new code state; a commit does not.

## The two suites

`ant testFast` runs about 2,100 tests in four tracks at once, in about 5 to 7 minutes:

- compiler: `CompilerJUTest` over `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/` and `parser_tests/`. It is the longest track, so it sets the total time.
- library: `LibraryJUTest` over `library_tests/`.
- othercompiler: `OtherCompilerJUTest` over `other_compiler_tests/`.
- misc: the unit `*JUTest` classes.

`ant testSystem` runs `SystemJUTest` over `ProjectFortress/tests/`, the interpreter's test folder. It runs about 680 tests in four shards, in about 2 to 4 minutes.

`ant testSpecData` runs the specification's 130 extracted examples (`SpecData/examples/basic`, `preliminaries`, `advanced`) under walk, in about a minute. The gate runs it after the two suites.

The newest gate summary has the exact counts and times of the last landed run:

    git log -1 --name-only --format= -- 'explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-*/gate/summary.txt'

The two suites work in the same way:

- Each suite runs `ant compileAll` first, as every `ant` test target does, so it never tests stale classes. After an edit of Java or Scala, that build empties `default_repository/caches` (`build-and-caches.md`, "Building"). Each analyses or compiles the Fortress code that it tests, in private caches.
- Each JVM gets 768 MB, a 32 MB stack and `FORTRESS_THREADS=4`, whatever the shell exports. The run steps of the compiled tests get `JAVA_FLAGS=-Xmx4g -Xss64m`, also whatever the shell exports.
- Each suite deletes `ProjectFortress/test-caches` when it starts. Each JVM keeps its caches in a folder of its own under it, so that the JVMs do not overwrite each other's entries. Temporary files go to `ProjectFortress/test-tmp/`.
- The results are in `ProjectFortress/TEST-RESULTS/fast-<track>/` and `system-<i>/`, as `TEST-<class>.txt`.

To run a suite:

- Run one suite at a time in a tree, because each suite deletes the `test-caches` that the other uses.
- Read the verdict in the line before `Total time:`: `BUILD SUCCESSFUL` means zero failures, and `BUILD FAILED` means at least one. Every `ant` test target ends with these lines, and exits non-zero when it failed.
- To compare test counts, compare the sum of the four shards. A file added to `tests/` moves every later file to another shard.
- If a suite's count fell, a `.test` file or a `tests=` line almost always went missing.

## The switches that the harness reads

Put a `-D` switch on the `java` line of a run by hand; the `java` line in `harness-one.sh` is a model. On the `ant` line, it does not reach the suites' JVMs.

- `-Dtests=<dir>`: the folder that `SystemJUTest` runs, in place of `tests/`.
- `-Dfortress.suite.shard=i/n`: run shard i of n only.
- `-Dfortress.unittests.count=N`: run N files at most.
- `-Dfortress.unittests.seed=<value>`: the order of the files. Each run prints its seed as `FORTRESS_UNITTESTS_SEED=...`.
- `FORTRESS_JUNIT_VERBOSE=1` for `SystemJUTest`, `-Dfortress.junit.verbose=true` for the compiled tests' classes: show the output of passing tests too.
- `-Dfortress.junit.reset=false`: `CompilerJUTest` and `LibraryJUTest` keep their caches folder. Without it, they empty it when they start.

## Outside the gate

- `ant testNotPassing` runs the interpreter programs of `ProjectFortress/not_passing_yet/`, which are expected to fail. It fails if one of them passes.
- No suite and no stage of the gate runs the team demos, the programs of `ProjectFortress/demos/`. Keep each of the 52 demos that `DemoTests` lists reaching its end (P-79). Check them with the demo driver below, not with `ant testDemos`, whose test of the output is weaker:
  - If your change edits walk, the parser, a phase that both paths run, a class under `nativeHelpers/` that a `builtinPrimitive` string of the interpreter's library names (`interpreter.md`, "Natives") or the interpreter's library, run the driver once, after your last edit of code.
  - Print the driver with `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/compile-ladder/rung-team-demos/REPORT.md#Commands worked out'`. Save the first script that it prints, under "The demo driver", without the text around it, as `tmp/run-demos.sh` in your tree.
  - From the tree's root, after you set up the call, run `bash tmp/run-demos.sh tmp/demos`. It runs long, so run it in the background with a log (`session.md`, "Long commands"). It runs the demos under walk one at a time and writes `tmp/demos/summary.tsv`.
  - The driver's last line of output, before the log's `EXIT=` line, must read 'demos: 52 run, 52 reached their end'. A demo reaches its end if it exits 0 and its output holds no "fail" in upper or lower case.
  - If your change breaks a demo and you know how to repair the demo, repair it in the commit of your change. Otherwise, report the demo, its output and the ledger row that holds the missing feature, as a defect that your change makes or uncovers.
- Nothing runs these folders: `not_working_compiler_tests/`, `not_working_library_tests/`, `not_working_static_tests/`, `obsolete_interpreter_tests/`, `long_term_not_working/`, `linker_tests/`, `compiler_regressions/`. Put every new test in a gated test folder. A test of a defect that fails today is an `XXX` test there (`tests-writing.md`).

## When to run a whole suite

- The gate runs every suite once, on the tree that lands (`gate.md`). Your brief says whether you run the gate.
- If your edit changes the Java or Scala of the checker, of walk, of a phase that both paths share or of such a class under `nativeHelpers/`, run all the tests that it reaches. Run them once, after your last edit of code. The run needs no commit.
  - For the checker, run `ant testQuick`: the compiler, othercompiler and library tracks at once (below).
  - For walk, run `ant testSystem`. It is the same as its four shards run by hand.
  - For a shared phase (under `compiler/`: name binding, DSL grammars, desugaring, the marking of overloaded calls in `OverloadRewriter`), the parser or such a class, run both.
- Quote the verdict lines and the command in your report, with the commit if your code is committed.
- If the gate later runs on a tree that holds other changes too, that tree is another code state. Your run and the gate's run do not repeat each other.
- After an edit of the code generator (`codegen/`, `OverloadSet`) or the runtime (`runtimeSystem/`), run your own tests, and the four-thread atomic runs (`gate.md`) if `compiler.md` asks for them. Leave the whole tracks to the gate.
- After every other change, run only your own tests, through the scripts below, and the demos where "Outside the gate" asks for them. Leave the rest to the gate. This includes an edit of either library, though it reaches many tests.

The suites do not check these:

- the bytecode optimizer, which nothing in the compiler calls;
- DSL grammars, except one program whose phases the misc track runs: `syntax_abstraction_tests/ForUse.fss`;
- the linker's aliasing of apis;
- `fortress unparse`;
- the round trip of the `.tfi` and `.tfs` caches;
- a behaviour above one thread that one run of each suite at four threads does not hit.

If your edit is in one of these, your own tests are its only check. Say so in your report.

## One test, or a few

Each script and `fortress junit` below ends with the verdict of JUnit's text runner: `OK (n tests)`, or `FAILURES!!!` with the counts. Read the verdict there: the exit code is 0 whatever the verdict.

### Interpreter tests

Run interpreter tests (`ProjectFortress/tests/`) from the tree's root, after you set up the call:

    explorations/compile-ladder/rung-inference-walk/harness-one.sh <tree>/tmp/h1 \
        ProjectFortress/tests/X.fss [ProjectFortress/tests/X.test] [more files ...]

- It runs `SystemJUTest` with testSystem's JVM settings, at `FORTRESS_THREADS=4`, on a folder that holds only the files that you name.
- It keeps its cache in the folder `<scratch-dir>.cache`. It starts from that cache while the build and the library sources are those that filled it. Otherwise, or with `COLD_CACHE=1`, it starts empty. Its first line says `cache filled` or `cache empty`.
- It runs the classes in `ProjectFortress/build/` and builds nothing. After you edit Java, Scala or a parser grammar, run `ant compileAll` first. If your tree has no build, seed it or build it as `worktrees.md` says.
- Give it a scratch directory that holds nothing else. The script deletes the directory when it starts and when it ends.
- If a test has an `X.test` file (its keys for a refusal at load), name it beside its `X.fss`.
- It takes 15 to 25 s with an empty cache, mostly to analyse the library, and about 4 s with a filled one. Name several files in one call to run them in one JVM.
- It shows the output of passing tests too, and removes the Java stack frames.

To see the whole diagnostic, with its Java stack, run the program directly, from `ProjectFortress/` as the harness does, because an import is looked up in the current directory first:

    cd ProjectFortress && ../bin/fortress -debug stacktrace tests/X.fss

The direct run and the harness use different heaps (`interpreter.md`, "Running a program").

### Compiled tests

Compiled tests are the `.test` files in `compiler_tests/`, `library_tests/` and `other_compiler_tests/`. They link with the library's jars in the tree's `default_repository/caches`. If a build started the caches again, or the tree's caches are empty, run the library order first (`build-and-caches.md`).

The script is `explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-N/merged-tests/junit.sh`. `climb-batch-N` is the folder's real name, not a placeholder. Run your own tree's copy: it runs the tree that it is in.

    ONE_JVM=1 explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-N/merged-tests/junit.sh <label> \
        ProjectFortress/compiler_tests X.test Y.test > <tree>/tmp/junit-<label>.txt 2>&1

- `<label>` is any word. It marks the run's lines in the output. The script writes to standard output only, so redirect it to your `tmp/`.
- With `ONE_JVM=1`, the whole list runs in one `fortress junit` run, in one JVM. The compile and link tests run before the run tests, as in the suite. Without `ONE_JVM=1`, each file gets its own JVM.
- It removes the named components' entries from the tree's `default_repository/caches` before the whole list and after it, not between files. So a link test and the run test that uses its jar pass in one call, with or without `ONE_JVM=1`.
- It runs the classes in `ProjectFortress/build/` and builds nothing, as `harness-one.sh` does.
- It removes the Java stack frames, and cuts each line at 240 characters.
- Its JVMs keep their temporary files in the tree's `tmp/`, and run at `FORTRESS_THREADS=4`.

To run the same list in one JVM without the script, and without its removal of cache entries:

    cd ProjectFortress && ../bin/fortress junit compiler_tests/X.test compiler_tests/Y.test

Run all the new files of one test folder together, in one JVM, as the suite does. A test that passes alone can fail beside others.

## One unit-test class, or one track

To run one unit-test class: `ant testOnly -DtestPattern=BitsJUTest`. It uses the tree's own caches and the shell's `FORTRESS_THREADS`.

To run tracks of testFast whole, run their target. Each target runs its tracks as testFast does, with the same JVMs and private caches:

- `ant testCompiler`: the compiler and othercompiler tracks.
- `ant testOtherCompiler`: the othercompiler track.
- `ant testLibrary`: the library track.
- `ant testQuick`: the three tracks.

Climb batch 32, rung D (rows 988 and 474). A top-level binding of several
names to a tuple, the form of the model program's hyperparameters,
stopped the compile: the checker left a node that it should have
replaced, typed each name so that it was accepted anywhere, and behind it
the code generator had no case for a left side of more than one name. The
checker now gives the rebuilt tuple the type of its checked elements, and
checks a declared name beside untyped ones against its element; the code
generator evaluates the right side once, into a hidden top-level
variable, at the first read of any name, and makes each name a top-level
variable of its own class. The model's lines 17 to 19 pass the code
generator. Rows 1026 to 1031 are new, and row 152 is noted.

This commit edits the original tree.

It still serves three callers: the two gatherings for the dispatch methods (`properlyInheritedMethodsNotIdenticallyCovered`, `CodeGen.java:499` and `:1147` at c1ce2a35e1) and `methodsNamed` (`:6784`). Type java/lang/Object ... is not assignable to ...$Late' in `mx?0`; at a trait instance the verifier passes, since it does not check assignment to an interface. ## Revival change

**The change.** The team's code generator (`compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java`, `dumpMethodChaining`, with `STypesUtil.removeIdenticallyCoveredMethods`, `scala_src/useful/STypesUtil.scala:1574`) wrote a forwarder for each inherited declaration with a body that no declaration of a subtype covered, comparing the two domains as schemas over each trait's own static parameters; it skipped every declaration without a body, an imported api's among them. So a compiled generic trait that declared again a method which it inherited through a trait that was not its first could not load, and a compiled object could not call a method whose body an imported api's trait gave it, unless that trait was first in its extends clause. The tree now writes one method for each such group, which runs the declaration of the lowest type that declares it, as walk does, and forwards to the api trait's body: `compiler_tests/TraitOwnMethodBesideInheritedCompiled`, `compiler_tests/ApiTraitMethodNotFirstCompiled`. A programmer no longer needs to put an api's trait first in an extends clause, or to keep a generic trait from declaring again what it inherits. Two limits stay: an object's own overloads of a functional method with self not first beside an inherited one still die at dispatch, and a body of a self-typed trait that returns `self` still fails verification at an object instance.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""The record's tool: it owns the form of FACTS.md and POSITIONS.md and of
their two history files, and is the only way to write them.

An entry is one line under a permanent number, `- F-87 **Title.** Text.` in
explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md and `- P-48 **Title.** Text.` in
POSITIONS.md. A number is never reused or changed: a new entry takes the
highest number its file has ever used, plus one. An entry stands under the
nearest `## ` or `### ` heading above it, its section. Its title is its bold
opening, or where it has none, its opening words up to the first colon,
semicolon or full stop.

A pointer is another entry's number in the sentence that needs it, alone
(`It builds P-48.`) or with the first words of the target's title in quotes
(`It builds P-48, "A type parameter the arguments do not fix ..."`, or
`P-48 ("...")`). Quoted words must open the target's current title (`...` or
`…` marks words left out); when an entry is retitled, the tool rewrites them
in every entry that points to it, in the same call.

The history (FACTS-history.md, POSITIONS-history.md beside the record) holds,
under `### F-87`, one block per change, oldest first: one provenance line (the
UTC time from the clock, the kind of change, `from` each report section,
`commit`, `by`, then the note after a colon), and the line as it stood before
the change. The tool derives the kind: `added`, `rewritten`, `moved to "S"`,
`merged into F-n`, `F-n merged in`, `removed`, `noted`; the numbering wrote one
`numbered` block per entry. A retitle that refreshed other entries' pointer
words, or a merge that moved their pointers, says so in one more line of the
block (`pointer words refreshed in: F-12, P-48`).

A `noted` block, which `note` writes, leaves the entry as it is. It adds what
the entry's history lacks, such as the curator's messages behind a text kept
word for word, with their times, or a correction of an earlier block. It holds
no earlier line, and its note says what it adds, so it needs one. A gone entry
takes none: its last block stays `merged into` or `removed`. A noted block
that corrects an earlier block names it by its time, in the field after the
kind: `correcting the block of 2026-10-13 19:07Z`, or, where blocks of the
entry share that minute, `correcting the 2nd block of 2026-10-14 04:41Z`,
counted oldest first. The block corrected is never edited.

Every write takes a lock (flock on .record.lock beside the record), checks the
state it would leave, appends the history blocks first and then replaces each
record file in one step. A write is refused only for what would break the
store: a bad number, a pointer that does not resolve or whose words do not
open its target's title, a line break in an entry, no provenance (neither
`--from` nor `--note`; for a noted block, no `--note`), a correction that
names no block or more than one, two blocks for one entry in one call.
Never for size. The tool does not commit: commit the record file and its
history together.

  PROVENANCE: --from PATH#HEADING (repeatable; PATH from the repository root

  resolves one), --commit HASH (in HEAD's history), --by WHO, --note WHY.
  Each write needs --from or --note.

# Facts on record

## Execution model

- F-7 **Walk and the compiled path share the parser and the phases, and only the compiled path runs the static type checker.** Walk switches the checker off, and no switch turns it on. So walk checks no static types of expressions: an ill-typed expression shows only when it runs, as a failed dispatch or as another run-time error, such as F-239's refusal of an `if` on a value that is not a `Boolean`. At load, walk refuses some ill-formed declarations: the `fortress-repo` skill's `interpreter.md`, "What walk checks", lists them, with their evidence in F-29 (`comprises` clauses), F-142 (the Meet 
- F-9 **`fortress typecheck` checks a program against the compiler's library, `Library/CompilerLibrary.fsi`, so it is no oracle for walk programs.** `Shell.java` calls `useCompilerLibraries()` for the command (row 69). P-12 has walk run the checker on its own programs after the switch-over, and walk cannot do so as it stands: it runs with type checking and the Scala checker off, the Java checker is gone (`compiler/StaticChecker.java:228-229`), and it has no case for the `CoercionInvocation` nodes that the checker inserts, by reading (row 833).
- F-11 **The code generator boxes every number, and boxing is the main representational cost of microGPT-shaped array code.** So a compiled `RR64` loop holds no `dadd` or `dmul` (the `fortress-repo` skill, "The compiled runtime"). In Java models of microGPT's three kernels, boxed elements cost 6.3× (dot product), 6.5× (matrix product) and 2.6× (row lift) over `double[]`. No such kernel compiles yet: the compiler prelude has no array type (row 305), and the arrays reach the compiled path with the one library (P-37). In a hot compiled loop, escape analysis removes the temporary boxes, and one
- F-12 **On the compiled path, the scalar `RR64` loop `bench1t` ran in 0.74 s in one session's measurement; the loop still pays for its generator, for boxing and for a transaction check at each use of its accumulator.** `bench1t` is `for i <- seq(1#20000000) do acc := acc 0.9999999 + 0.0000001 end` on a `var acc: RR64`, with both literals written in the loop. The time is the median of three loop-only runs at one thread (`compile-ladder/rung0/REPORT.md`, "The four timings"). Times taken in different sessions differ on this machine, so compare only times from one session. What the loop does, rea
- F-17 **The bytecode cache can come up empty after a library order that reports exit 0.** Running the same commands again, one at a time, made the jars. The cause is not known. Check the five jars before a compiled run (the `fortress-repo` skill's `build-and-caches.md`, "The library order"). Detail: `perf-probes/boxing/REPORT.md` section 1.
- F-18 **On the compiled path, the class loader makes the class of a generic instantiation at its first use, by rewriting the template's bytecode with ASM, and the rewriting only renames, so it gives no instance a `double[]` field.** The class is `InstantiatingClassloader`; the `fortress-repo` skill's "The compiled runtime" gives the mechanism. A size is part of the made class's name, as in `pNatMeth$Box⟦3⟧`, the object `Box` at size 3 in the probe component `pNatMeth`. Inside the class, the size's descriptor is `RTTIsize.of("<n>")` (F-129). A field of the template's type `T`, `LT;`, becom
- F-19 **By the specification, the iterations of a `for` loop, the elements of a tuple, and the arguments of a call or an operator may run in parallel, and a program must assume that they do.** A `for` loop is sequential only if every generator is, as `seq(g)` or `sequential(g)` makes it. An implementation may also run them one after another (`evaluation/parallelism.tex:88-90`), so a program cannot count on parallel runs either. For the elements of a tuple and the operands of an operator, each path starts a task only where it judges it worth it: walk by `TupleTask.worthSpawning`, which also go
- F-20 **Sizes, the `nat` and `int` static parameters, are values at run time; they check shapes, and no optimization uses them (F-40, what a size costs at run time).** The compiled checker checks them (F-67), and a sized program loads and runs compiled (F-129). Under walk, `Vector` and `Matrix` take their sizes from an array built at run time: `f[\nat s\](v: Vector[\RR64,s\])` takes `s` from `array[\RR64\](3)`, and overloads on `Vector` and `Matrix` dispatch by rank (row 214). The array-type syntax `T[n]` with a `nat` parameter does not unify with such an array, "Cannot unify … with ArrayTy
- F-21 **The February 2011 Working Draft's bare `Nothing`, one object for every `T`, is accepted on neither path: the grammar refuses its `excludes` clause, and without that clause `T` is undefined.** The declaration is `object Nothing extends Maybe[\T\] excludes Just[\T\] where {T extends Object}` (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic-lib/convenience.tex:40`). Both paths stop at a syntax error at `excludes`, since an object has no `excludes` clause (measured: `reviews/spec-refused-examples.md`, E4). Without that clause, both report `T is undefined` at the `T` of the `extends` clause: a `where` cla
- F-22 **When a component's name differs from the api that it exports, neither path finds the component, for an exported function or variable alike.** The specification resolves an imported api to any component that exports it (`Specification/basic/components/overview.tex`). The tree looks only under the api's name, unless a user maps the api to its component by hand with `LinkShell`'s `alink` or `clink`. The linker's component repository looks this way (`Linker.whoIsImplementingMyAPI`), so `fortress link` and walk print "Could not find an implementation for API … on path" before any code is

# Rung L, rung-label-exit: the record lines

## For FACTS

**The compiled path runs `label` and `exit`: an exit is a thrown `LabelExit` that names one evaluation of its label block, and reaches it from a loop's body and from another task.** `CodeGen.forLabel` keeps a new `LabelExit.Target` in an immutable local under the label's name and takes, in a handler, the exits that name it; `CodeGen.forExit` throws `LabelExit.of(value, target)` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java:1776-1857`, `runtimeSystem/LabelExit.java`). A function expression or a task whose body exits captures the target as it captures any immutable variable, because every identifier counts as a free variable (`compiler/codegen/FreeVariables.java:98`) and the checker lets no variable share a label's name (`scala_src/typechecker/impls/Misc.scala:704`). A group of forked arms joins the arms that it forked before the exit passes it: at four threads every forked iteration of a parallel `for` runs to its end or to its own exit, and the label's value is the exit of the first arm in the arms' order; at one thread the iterations after the exit do not run. No `catch` clause takes an exit. What it means for the work: the one library's `Indexed.indexOf` compiles in its own form (the test's `Holder.indexOf`), and row 81's wall is gone. Four limits stand, each with its test: an exit out of an `atomic` block loses the block's writes (NEW-L-1); a `finally` clause on the exit's way does not run (row 890); a label block as a call's later argument fails verification (row 322); a label block whose value joins a numeral with a number stops the code generator (row 340), so a number beside an exit's value is bound to a typed variable first. Test: `compiler_tests/LabelExitCompiled`, which fails with 'Can't compile Label' without the two members. Detail: `explorations/compile-ladder/rung-label-exit/REPORT.md`, "What changed and why" and "Points to report reached".

Row 890, a note (it fits: 1 character of the notes and 34 of the row are left with it):

| 322 | an `atomic do … end` block, a `try … catch` or a `label` block as a call's argument after the first, where the arguments run in order, produces a class that fails verification on the compiled path: `VerifyError`, the stack's size at a branch target | NEGATIVE-VERIFIED | implementation gap (codegen) | `Specification/basic/expressions/atomic.tex`, "Atomic Expressions"; `Specification/basic/expressions/try.tex`, "Try Expressions" | `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/XXXAtomicBlockLaterArgument.test` | ours | siblings: 526. `CodeGen.forAtomicBlock`, `forTry` and `forLabel` branch from a handler, which clears the operand stack, to a label reached with the earlier arguments on it, so each is right only on an empty stack. `two(k, atomic do … end)`, `two(k, try boomVal(k) catch e Boom => e.code end)` and `two(k, label out … end out)` fail when the class loads; the test's `bump`, `caught` and `left`. The team's code generator had no case for a label block or an exit: `CodeGen` declared no `forLabel` and no `forExit`, so the node reached `defaultCase`, which refused the declaration with 'Can't compile Label' (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java:1859`, `defaultCase`). # Rung A, rung-atomic-expr-field: the record lines

Code and tests: commit `67b1030c48` on `wip/rung-atomic-expr-field`; the gather's commit on `main` takes its place in the closes below. Detail and every quoted run: `explorations/compile-ladder/rung-atomic-expr-field/REPORT.md`.

## Findings

1. **The code generator compiles an atomic expression.** `atomic e`, for a body `e` that is no `do` block, is compiled as the atomic block that holds `e` alone, the node the parser makes for `atomic do e end`; the new member emits no instruction of its own (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java:1870-1877`). Holds for every body the checker accepts but a lone numeral at a place of declared type, as `f(): ZZ32 = atomic 1`, which fails verification (NEW-A-1, below; the skeptic's correction); the expression has the block's limits, among them a `VerifyError` as a call's argument after the first (row 322). Evidence: `compiler_tests/AtomicExprCompiled` (on the base: 'Can't compile AtomicExpr at ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/AtomicExprCompiled.fss:8.9'; on the change: PASS at one thread and at four). For the work: `Library/OneShotFlag.fss:18` is no longer a wall of the code generator; `tryatomic` still is (row 353).
2. **An object's `var` field, a `var` value parameter among them, is inside the transaction of an `atomic` block on the compiled path.** The object's JVM field is `public final` and holds a `MutableFValue` cell; a read and a write emit a top-level `var`'s code on that cell (`VarCodeGen.java:202-239`, `:313-410`; `CodeGen.java:4827-4850`, `:4865-4903`). Holds for a value parameter, a field of the body, and a generic object's value parameter whose type is the type parameter (run at `String`, a tuple type and an arrow type). An immutable field holds its value and reads by the same two instructions as before. Evidence: `compiler_tests/AtomicFieldCompiled` (old code at four threads: 'value parameter 39220 (expected 40000), body field 67439 (expected 80007), torn reads 1, generic value parameter 39313 (expected 40000)'; the change: PASS at one thread and at four, and in three runs of the atomic loop). For the work: the one library's `OneShot`, `Box[\T\](var val: T)` and `String.fss`'s var fields are tracked once the compiled path reads them.
3. **A loop body or a function expression inside an object's method reads and writes the object's `var` field itself.** On the base each captured a copy of the value when it was built, so `fill(k) = for i <- 1#k do atomic do n := n + 1 end end` in the object left `n` unchanged at one thread too, and a function expression read a stale value and lost its writes. The cell is captured now, as a top-level `var`'s is, because a var field's `VarCodeGen` is a `MutableStaticBinding` (`VarCodeGen.java:207`; the three sites that ask are `CodeGen.java` `createTaskLexEnvVariables`, `taskConstructorDesc` and `constructWithFreeVars`). The defect had no ledger row. Evidence: `compiler_tests/VarFieldCapturedCompiled` (old code: 'a function's reads 11 and 11 (expected 11 and 10), after a function's write 10 (expected 15), after a loop's writes 5 (expected 1007)'; the change: PASS). For the work: an immutable field is still captured by value, which is right.
4. **Every read and write of a `var` field now pays the transaction check and one indirection,** outside `atomic` too, as a mutable local and a top-level `var` do (row 641). Not timed. The two microGPT programs and the compiler's prelude declare no object with a var field (`grep` for `var` in an object's header or body over `explorations/run-c4/src/*.fss`, `explorations/apl/mg/*.fss` and the four prelude components finds only local variables).
5. **A `value` object with a `var` field compiles, and its `SEQV` changed.** `value object V(var n: ZZ32)`: `V(1) === V(1)` was `true` and is `false`, because `SEQV` compares a value object's JVM fields and a cell equals only itself (`nativeHelpers/equalityRule.java:83`). The specification forbids the declaration (`Specification/basic/objects.tex:35`); nothing refuses it on either path (row 112).
6. **`ant testQuick` on `67b1030c48`:** compiler 1625, othercompiler 263, library 86, no failure, `BUILD SUCCESSFUL`, 7 minutes 2 seconds. The atomic loop of gate.md with `AtomicExprCompiled`, `AtomicFieldCompiled` and `VarFieldCapturedCompiled` added: 75 of 75 runs PASS at four threads. The distance stage's shadow patch applies: exit 0.

## For FACTS

**A compiled object's `var` field lives in a cell that the object holds, and an atomic expression is its body in an atomic block.** On the compiled path a `var` value parameter or `var` field of an object is a `MutableFValue` cell in a `public final` JVM field, made by the constructor; each read and write checks `BaseTask.inATransaction()` and goes through the transaction or the cell, by the code of a top-level `var` (`VarCodeGen.MutableFieldVar`, a `MutableStaticBinding`), and a loop body or a function expression in the object's method captures the cell. A field without `var` holds its value and has no check. `atomic e` is compiled by `forAtomicBlock` on the block that holds `e`. What it means: a change of the transaction's variable code reaches fields with no second edit, and a new kind of nested context must capture a var field's cell as it does a top-level `var`'s. Tests: `compiler_tests/AtomicFieldCompiled`, `compiler_tests/VarFieldCapturedCompiled`, `compiler_tests/AtomicExprCompiled`. Detail: `explorations/compile-ladder/rung-atomic-expr-field/REPORT.md`, "What changed and why" and "The bytecode".

## Handover

Rung A landed on its branch at `67b1030c48`: the compiled path compiles `atomic e` and keeps an object's `var` field in a cell that a transaction tracks and that a loop body or a function expression captures; rows 875 and 319 close, row 641 takes a new line, row 112 a note; the gate's atomic runs gain `AtomicExprCompiled` and `AtomicFieldCompiled`, and `VarFieldCapturedCompiled` can join them; `tryatomic` (row 353), an atomic block or expression as a later argument (row 322) and plain writes beside a block (row 948) stand as they were; a numeral as the value of an atomic expression at a place of declared type waits for the checker (NEW-A-1).

## Revival change

### The change

- **An atomic expression compiles.** The team's code generator compiled `atomic do ... end` and had no case for `atomic e` over any other body: its `defaultCase` refused the node, 'Can't compile AtomicExpr' (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java:1776` and `forAtomicBlock` at `:1835`, at `c1ce2a35e1`). The tree now compiles `atomic e` as the atomic block that holds `e`, with the value of `e` (`compiler_tests/AtomicExprCompiled`). The reason: the specification gives the atomic expression its body's value and makes all its reads and writes one step (`Specification/basic/expressions/atomic.tex`, section "Atomic Expressions"), walk runs it, and the one library writes it (`Library/OneShotFlag.fss:18`). Where the body's value is a numeral at a place of declared type, write `atomic do ... end`: the checker refuses `atomic if c then 1 else 0 end` there, and `atomic 1` fails the JVM's verification (ledger row NEW-A-1).
- **A compiled object's `var` field is tracked by a transaction, at the cost of a check on every access.** The team's code generator read an object's field with a bare `GETFIELD` and wrote it with a bare `PUTFIELD`, a `var` field as any other (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/codegen/VarCodeGen.java:174-236` at `c1ce2a35e1`), so an `atomic` block did not track it: 40,000 `atomic do n := n + 1 end` on a field from a parallel loop gave 34,631 to 39,313 at four threads. The tree now keeps a `var` value parameter or `var` field in a cell that the object holds, read and written as a top-level `var` is; each access, outside `atomic` too, first asks whether a transaction is running (`compiler_tests/AtomicFieldCompiled`). A field without `var` is as it was. The reason: mutable fields of reference objects are mutable locations (`Specification/basic/evaluation/memory-ops.tex`, section "Memory and Memory Operations"), an atomic expression's reads and writes are all one step, and walk is exact on the same program.
- **A loop body or a function expression in an object's method works on the object's `var` field, not on a copy.** The team's code generator gave each task and closure a copy of a field's value, made when the task or closure was built, so a write from a loop body in the object's own method was lost, at one thread too, and a function expression read a stale value: `for i <- 1#k do atomic do n := n + 1 end end` in a method left `n` at 0. The tree now gives the task or closure the field's cell (`compiler_tests/VarFieldCapturedCompiled`). The reason: the measured failure, and walk's result on the same program.
- **Do not give a `value` object a `var` field in a compiled program.** The specification forbids it (`Specification/basic/objects.tex`, section "Value Objects") and nothing refuses it; with the field in a cell, two such objects built alike are no longer strictly equivalent, `V(1) === V(1)` is `false`.

### Provenance

- The atomic expression: ledger row 875; the batch record `explorations/coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-31.md`, rung A; climb batch 31.
- The field in a cell: ledger row 319; fork A1 of `explorations/coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-31.md`, "Forks the batch takes", whose default it builds ("A `var` field is kept in a cell, as a top-level `var` is"); P-169, whose store and slots are untouched; climb batch 31, rung A.
- The captured cell: measured by rung A of climb batch 31 while building fork A1; no row; a consequence of A1's default.
- The value object: ledger row 112, with the note above.

# Rung V, rung-walk-value-bound: the record lines

Code commit: fcdf7bc2da on `wip/rung-walk-value-bound`, cut from c1ce2a35e1. Detail: `explorations/compile-ladder/rung-walk-value-bound/REPORT.md`.

## Findings

1. **Walk's check of value types passes the symbolic type of a type parameter.** Claim: `FTraitOrObject.enforceValueness` refuses a declared trait or object that is not a value type below a value type, and no longer refuses the symbolic type that walk makes for a type parameter. Conditions: under walk; a generic method of a trait whose type parameter is bounded by the trait's static parameter, at an instance at a value object, and an overloaded function's own type parameter bounded by a value object (`dup[\T extends NN32\](a: T)` beside a second `dup` stopped at load on the base with the same message; declared alone it ran). Evidence: `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/evaluator/types/FTraitOrObject.java:102-103`; `ProjectFortress/tests/TraitGenericMethodValueBoundWalk.fss` failed on the base ('T@...: non-value subtype of value type RR32') and passes; `ProjectFortress/tests/OverloadedGenericValueBoundWalk.fss`, the skeptic's, failed on the base ('T@...: non-value subtype of value type NN32') and passes; `ProjectFortress/tests/NonValueBelowValueTypeWalk.fss` holds the refusal of a declared object. Meaning: the merge of the five number types with their objects meets no stop at a bound that is one of them.
2. **Walk's load check reads a generic declaration beside a plain one over an object type by the Return Type Rule.** Claim: an own generic beside a declaration without static parameters, whose domain some instance of the generic holds, is no longer taken to exclude it because the lists differ at object types; the pair is read on its declared domains, and the plain result is compared at every instance of the generic that applies to an argument of the plain declaration, which an object type at a parameter of the returned type parameter bounds from below. Conditions: under walk, at load; neither list with a varargs parameter, lists of one length; a more specific declaration that writes no return type is not judged; a `comprises` clause is not read; two plain lists that differ at an object type keep the shortcut (row 697). Evidence: `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/evaluator/values/OverloadedFunction.java:513-527`, `:814-820`, `:837`, `:862`, `:882-903`; `ProjectFortress/tests/GenericBesidePlainObjectReturnRuleWalk.fss` failed on the base (it printed `plain`, 'Missing expected refusal at load') and passes; the guards `GenericBesidePlainObjectValidWalk.fss` and `GenericBesidePlainObjectNoReturnTypeWalk.fss` pass before and after; `ant testSystem` on the final code: 861 tests in four shards, 0 failures, `BUILD SUCCESSFUL`. Meaning: once `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `ZZ`, `NN64` and `RR64` are objects, walk refuses an invalid pair over them as it does today over the traits, and loads the valid pair of row 550.

**The change.** The team's walk takes two overloaded parameter lists to exclude each other wherever every parameter at which they differ is an object type of one of them (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/evaluator/values/OverloadedFunction.java:511` at c1ce2a35e1, the team's `distinct |= unequal && (allObjInstance1 || allObjInstance2)`), and so compares no return types for such a pair. # Rung X, rung-return-rule-object: record lines

## Findings

1. **The compiled checker's Return Type Rule counts, at an object type, only the instances whose domain meets.** Claim: for `f` more specific than `g`, `satisfiesReturnTypeRule` reads a type parameter `T` of `g` that the domains do not force, where `T` is a whole parameter type of `g` and `f` has an object type `C` at that position, as `T ∪ C` in `g`'s domain and return type; every other instance is compared as before. Conditions: `C` is an object type, with or without static arguments, or the self type of one; a parameter inside a static argument, a size, and a position where `f` has a trait, a tuple or a function type are unchanged. Evidence: `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/overloading/OverloadingOracle.scala:114-122`, `:136-167`; `compiler_tests/OverloadReturnObjectDomain` (compile, link, run), which the base's code refused, 'the return type of Circle->Circle'; `XXXOverloadReturnObjectDomainOtherType` still refused; `ant testFast` BUILD SUCCESSFUL (compiler 1624, othercompiler 263, library 86, no failure); the count stage's table and `run.txt` equal to the base's, the distance `DISTANCE SAME 0`. What it means: once each built-in number type is one value object (P-178), a generic declaration that returns its type parameter beside a declaration on `ZZ32`, `ZZ64` or `RR64` that returns that type passes the rule.

2. **A dispatcher whose range is a static parameter casts each arm's result to that range.** Claim: `OverloadSet` emits the cast in `generateCall` and `generateLeafCall` where the dispatcher's principal declaration returns one of its static parameters and the arm declares another return type; for an arm instantiated at run time it takes the place of the cast to the arm's declared return type. Conditions: every other dispatcher writes the bytecode it wrote before. Evidence: `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/OverloadSet.java:1800`, `:1830`, `:1947`, `:1958-1971`; without it `bin/fortress run OverloadReturnObjectDomain` dies, 'VerifyError: Bad return type ... Type OverloadReturnObjectDomain$Circle (current frame, stack[0]) is not assignable to OverloadReturnObjectDomain$Square'; with it the `run` step passes at one thread and at four. What it means: the pair that the checker now accepts runs; the verification failure that row 496's notes name for `k(x: ZZ64): ZZ64` beside `k[\T\](x: T): T` has this cause, and was not run again here.

3. **Row 542's second pair, as written, is refused by the positional rule.** Claim: `keep[\T\](x: T): T` beside `keep[\U extends Object\](x: Box[\U\]): Box[\U\]` passes the Return Type Rule and is refused, 'the static parameters of ... should correspond position by position'. Conditions: both declarations have one static parameter of their own; as a functional method `keep(self): Box[\U\]` of `object Box[\U\]`, or with a different number of static parameters, the pair compiles and runs. Evidence: `compiler_tests/XXXOverloadGenericObjectDomainByPosition.test:3`; `OverloadReturnObjectDomain.fss:9-11`, `:16`; `OverloadingOracle.scala:201-215`. What it means: P-45's positional rule, not the Return Type Rule, is what stands between that spelling and a compiled run.

4. **The checker's time is unchanged.** Claim: the count stage took 93.6 s on the base build and 93.2 s on the change, one run each in one session, with equal tables and equal `run.txt`; a JFR profile of the change holds 0 of 5,921 samples in the new member. Evidence: REPORT.md, "The stages and the checker's time". What it means: no second-pass change was due.

## For FACTS

- **F-75, rewritten in its last sentences.** The fact as it stands: the compiled checker's Return Type Rule compares every instance of the less specific declaration, except that a type parameter standing as a whole parameter type where the more specific declaration has an object type is read as its union with that object type, so that only the instances whose domain meets the object are compared (the type group's 2011 paper sets aside the instances whose domain is `Bottom`). It accepts `ident[\T\](x: T): T` beside `ident(x: Circle): Circle`, `Circle` an object, and the pair runs. What it means: the merge of the built-in number types with their objects (P-178) does not bring a refusal to pairs over them. Test: `compiler_tests/OverloadReturnObjectDomain`, which accepts and runs; `XXXOverloadReturnObjectDomainOtherType`, `XXXOverloadReturnEveryInstance`, which pin the rule's refusals; `XXXOverloadGenericObjectDomainByPosition` and `XXXOverloadPermutedStaticParams`, which pin the positional rule's. The entry's words "it also refuses a generic declaration beside a plain one whose domain is an object type ... (row 542, open)" and "`XXXOverloadReturnObjectDomain`, which pins row 542's" no longer hold. Detail: `explorations/compile-ladder/rung-return-rule-object/REPORT.md`, "What changed and why".

- **New fact: a compiled dispatcher of a generic declaration casts an arm's result to its own range.** The fact: where an overload set's principal declaration returns one of its static parameters, the dispatcher that `OverloadSet` writes casts the result of each arm with another declared return type to that parameter, which the class loader instantiates. What it means: a generic declaration beside a declaration on an object type verifies at every instance; a dispatcher whose range is no static parameter has no such cast (row 699). Test: the `run` step of `compiler_tests/OverloadReturnObjectDomain`. Detail: REPORT.md, "What changed and why", "The dispatcher's return".

## Ledger

- **Row 542: close**, by commit f145926e3b and test `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/OverloadReturnObjectDomain.test`. Its reproducer `XXXOverloadReturnObjectDomain` is renamed to that test.
- **Row 853**: not this rung's; unchanged.

The pair is valid: the Return Type Rule holds at every instance whose domain meets `Duo[\U, V\]`, and the two differ in their number of static parameters, so the positional rule does not apply. The crash is in the type check of the call, before the overloading check: `STypesUtil.isDynamicallyApplicable` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/useful/STypesUtil.scala:1196` at f145926e3b) asks whether the second declaration's domain, still holding `V`, is a subtype of the best arrow's. With one static parameter (`Box[\U\]`) the call type-checks. `keep(Square)` alone compiles and runs. Not tried under walk. |

No gated test: rung V of this batch edits the check, and a test green while walk loads the pair could turn red on the merged tree. |

- **F-75, one more sentence** beside the rewriting above: at a tuple of object types the rule still compares the instances that cannot meet, and refuses `ident[\T\](x: T): T` beside `ident(x: (Circle, Circle)): (Circle, Circle)` (NEW-X-3); test `compiler_tests/XXXOverloadReturnTupleDomain`.
- **The specification.** `Specification/appendices/changes.tex`, the same sentence of the Effect: it no longer says that the rule counts only the instances that meet, which holds at an object type only; it now says so of an object type and names the tuple pair as still refused. It names no row: the gather puts NEW-X-3's number there if the passage's other sentences keep theirs.

On the base's code the run prints `g Circle` and dies, 'VerifyError: Bad return type'; on this branch it prints `g Circle`, `g generic`, `PASS`. ## The specification

`Specification/appendices/changes.tex:3097-3104`, the Effect of the revival's overloading entry: the sentence that named row 542 now says that the compiled checker's Return Type Rule counts only the instances whose parameter type meets the more specific declaration's, and that the pair on an object type compiles and runs. No other sentence is made false. The specification was not built on this branch.

## Handover line

Rung X: the compiled Return Type Rule accepts a generic declaration beside a declaration on an object type (row 542 closes, test `OverloadReturnObjectDomain`), and the pair runs through a cast in the dispatcher (`OverloadSet.java`, a file beyond those named); count 0, distance 0, the checker's time unchanged (93.6 s, 93.2 s); row 542's second pair as written stays refused by P-45's positional rule; two new rows, NEW-X-1 (a checker crash on a two-parameter generic object) and NEW-X-2.

## Revival change

**The change.** The team's compiled checker tested the Return Type Rule at one instance of the less specific declaration, the solution of the domains (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/overloading/OverloadingOracle.scala:81-95` at a874948ac), and so accepted `ident[\T\](x: T): T` beside `ident(x: Circle): Circle`, `Circle` an object; the team's code generator returned an arm's result from the dispatcher without a cast (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/OverloadSet.java:1865-1866` at a874948ac), and the class of the generic declaration's instance at another object type failed the JVM's verification, `VerifyError: Bad return type`. The tree now compares every instance of the less specific declaration whose domain meets the more specific one's: where the more specific declaration's parameter type is an object type and the other's is a type parameter, only the instances at which the parameter holds the object. It accepts the pair, refuses `g[\T\](x: T): T` beside `g(x: Circle): String`, and the dispatcher casts an arm's result to its range where that range is a static parameter, so the pair runs and each call runs the most specific declaration that takes its argument. Tests: `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/OverloadReturnObjectDomain` (accepts, runs) and `XXXOverloadReturnObjectDomainOtherType` (refuses). The reason: the Return Type Rule speaks of argument types other than `BottomType` (`Specification/advanced/overloading.tex:555-559`), an object trait type excludes any type that is not its supertype (`Specification/basic/types-vals-vars.tex:288`), and the type group's paper sets aside the instances of the special arrow whose domain is `Bottom` (`Papers/Types/overloading-check.tick:180`); the verifier's refusal is quoted in the report.

**Provenance.** Row 542 of the gap ledger; fork X1 of `explorations/coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-31.md`, "Forks the batch takes", a default built under P-45 and for P-178; climb batch 31, run 1, rung X. The cast in `OverloadSet.java` is the worker's choice, reported as a file edited beyond those named.

Applied patch to 'ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/SelfTypeReturnSelfRun.fss' cleanly.

# Rung K, rung-comprises-cast: record lines

Base `c1ce2a35e1`; the code and tests are commit `34fb6364d6` and the skeptic's fix `f9bc4f2546`, the specification's sentence commit `3139c8db39`, on `wip/rung-comprises-cast`.

## Findings

1. **The compiled code casts `self` where it stands at a type below its trait.** Claim: where an expression has self's type (the checker's `TraitSelfType` with a non-empty list: a trait whose `comprises` clause lists types, or a trait with a self-type parameter; a typecase whose arms each have it, which the checker types as a union of it, counts) and the declared type is a trait type or a type variable that is a strict subtype of the trait, the code generator emits a cast to the declared type. Conditions: at a single argument of a function, a method or a constructor (`CodeGen.evalArg`), at a typed binding and an assignment (`forExprsSerial`), and at a method's returned value (`generateActualMethodCode`, for a trait's default body, an object's method, a top-level function and a generic method); not where the trait lists a type at a `where`-clause variable. Evidence: `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java:7308-7331` and its calls at `:3011`, `:5397`, `:7289`; `compiler_tests/ComprisesValueAtListedTypeCompiled` and `compiler_tests/SelfTypeReturnSelfRun`, each `VerifyError` on the base and `PASS` after; `ant testFast` on `34fb6364d6`: 'Tests run: 1627, Failures: 0', 'BUILD SUCCESSFUL'. Meaning: `trait QQ comprises { Ratio }` of the one library, which passes `self` to `numerator` and `denominator` on 23 lines, no longer fails verification for that reason once a program compiles against it; that is not yet shown by a run, since no program compiles against the one library.

2. **Only `self` gets the reading.** Claim: the compiled checker lets a value stand at a listed type only where the value has self's type; a variable declared at the trait is refused. Conditions: `q: Q = R(1, 2)`, then `den(q)` for `den(r: R)` and `trait Q comprises { R }`. Evidence: `bin/fortress compile` of that program prints 'Could not check call to function den' and 'R->ZZ32 is not applicable to an argument of type Q.' Also `typecase self of Disc => discArea(self)` is refused in `trait Shape comprises { Disc, Square }`: 'Disc->ZZ32 is not applicable to an argument of type (Shape & {Disc, Square})'; with a binder, `c: Disc => discArea(c)`, it compiles and ran on the base. Meaning: the cast's test can read the expression's type alone, and asks the type analyzer nothing at any other argument.

3. **The cast keeps the bytecode of a place where the value's type is a subtype of the declared type, and adds a cast at one kind of place that verified on the base.** Claim: no cast is added where the value's type is a subtype of the declared type by `extends`. A cast is added, where the base emitted none and the class verified, for a value of self's type at a declared trait type strictly below self's trait: the verifier does not check an interface type, so such a place ran on the base. Evidence: `javap -c -p` of every class of a program of upcasting calls, bindings and returns (`takeT(O)`, `t: T = O`, `widen(o: O): T = o`, `up(): T = self`, `takeT(self)` in `trait T`), compiled by the base build and by `34fb6364d6`: `diff` prints nothing over 336 lines. The three jars of the compiler's library hold the same counts on the base, on `34fb6364d6` and on `f9bc4f2546`: `fortress.CompilerBuiltin` 2149 lines with `checkcast` or `castTo` of 15996 instructions, `fortress.CompilerLibrary` 466 of 4620, `fortress.CompilerAlgebra` 1 of 160. For `trait Q comprises { M }`, `trait M extends Q comprises { R1, R2 }` and `mid(m: M)`, the default bodies `mid(self)`, `asMid(): M = self` and `m: M = self` each gain `checkcast …$M` (three hunks of `diff` over the two `javap` outputs), and the program prints `2 2 2 PASS` on the base and after. `compiler_tests/SelfTypeReturnSelfAtTraitRun` is the gated case of the kind: it ran on the base and runs after. Meaning: fork K1's "a call that verifies today keeps its bytecode" holds at an object type and not at a trait type below self's trait; the cast there cannot fail, since the checker's reading says the value has the type.

4. **A cast at the checker's type of a `where`-clause size names no class.** Claim: for `mk(): NatParamT` passed to `size[\nat n\](x: Nt[\n\])`, the declared type the code generator sees is `Nt[\n#3\]`, the checker's own variable. Evidence: a form of the cast without the `opensSizes` test turned `compiler_tests/XXXNatOpenRun` from 'VerifyError: Bad type on operand stack' to 'NumberFormatException: For input string: "n#3"'. Meaning: row 307's repair needs the value's own size at run time, not this cast; the landed form leaves the test as it was.

5. **Asking the type analyzer at every argument stops a link that passes today.** Claim: `NodeComparator.compare` of two types with a `bool` static argument throws 'subtypeCompareTo(class com.sun.fortress.nodes.BoolArg class com.sun.fortress.nodes.BoolArg) is not implemented!'. Evidence: `ant testFast` on the first form of the cast, 'Tests run: 1627, Failures: 2', both `XXXBoolStaticArgRun` (its link through `BoolStaticArgRunLink`, and its run). Meaning: a later cast site in the code generator gates on the expression's type before it compares types.

## For FACTS

**The compiled code casts `self` where the checker reads it as a listed type or as the self-type parameter.** `CodeGen.castToTypeBelow` casts a value that has self's type to a declared type strictly below its trait, at a single argument, a typed binding, an assignment and a method's returned value, also where the value is a typecase whose arms each have self's type; a closure's returned value and a conditional's arms get none (rows NEW-K-1, NEW-K-2), and a trait that lists a type at a `where`-clause variable gets none (row 307). Source: `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java:7308-7331`. Tests: `compiler_tests/ComprisesValueAtListedTypeCompiled`, `compiler_tests/SelfTypeReturnSelfRun`. Detail: `explorations/compile-ladder/rung-comprises-cast/REPORT.md`, "What changed and why".

F-225's sentence "A compiled default body that returns `self` dies at class load with a `VerifyError` when the trait's self-type parameter is an object type ... an open defect (row 695)" no longer holds: the body runs (`compiler_tests/SelfTypeReturnSelfRun`); a function expression or a local function that returns `self` so still dies (row NEW-K-1).

## Ledger

- Close row 991: commit `34fb6364d6`, test `ComprisesValueAtListedTypeCompiled`.
- Close row 695: commit `34fb6364d6`, test `SelfTypeReturnSelfRun` (`compiler_tests/XXXSelfTypeReturnSelfRun.fss` and `.test` renamed; `SelfTypeReturnSelfRunLink.test` now names the plain component). The row's notes also hold a `ClassCircularityError`, which the rung does not repair: it goes on as row NEW-K-3 below.
- Rows 307 and 815: no change; no test of theirs changed. `XXXNatOpenRun` and `XXXFunctionalMethodComprisedObject` fail as before.
- New rows, section "12. The compiled path: constructs, crashes and the switch-over". Each was linted with `explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py check --rows`; each fails only the number rule.

| NEW-K-1 | a compiled function expression or local function that returns `self` at a type that its trait's `comprises` clause lists, or as the trait's self-type parameter, fails the JVM's verification when the closure's class loads: `fn (): R => self` in `trait Q comprises { R }` | NEGATIVE-VERIFIED | implementation gap (codegen) | `basic/traits.tex`, "Trait Declarations" | `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/XXXComprisesValueFromClosureRun.test` | climb batch 31 rung K | siblings: 991, 695. 'VerifyError: Bad return type … $\=fn@….apply()L…$R; … Type …$Q (current frame, stack[0]) is not assignable to …$R'. `CodeGen.forFnExpr` and `forLetFn` return the body's value with no cast; a method's returned value gets one (`castToTypeBelow`, `compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java`). The checker accepts it and the link is clean (`ComprisesValueFromClosureRunLink`). The same for `fn (): S => self` in `trait Shape[\S extends Shape[\S\]\]`. Workaround: bind `self` at the listed type first, `r: R = self`, and return `r`. |

| NEW-K-2 | a compiled conditional with `self` in one arm and a value of the listed type in the other, at a type that the `comprises` clause of self's trait lists, fails the JVM's verification at class load: `chosen(c: Boolean): R = if c then self else R(0, 0) end` in `trait Q comprises { R }` | NEGATIVE-VERIFIED | implementation gap (codegen) | `basic/traits.tex`, "Trait Declarations" | `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/XXXComprisesValueAtConditionalArmRun.test` | climb batch 31 rung K | siblings: 991. 'VerifyError: Bad return type … Q$DefaultTraitMethods.chosen … Type java/lang/Object (current frame, stack[0]) is not assignable to …$R'. The arms leave the trait's interface and the object's class on the stack, which the verifier merges to `Object`; the cast of a returned value (`CodeGen.castToTypeBelow`) reads the conditional's static type, which is not self's, and emits nothing. With `self` in both arms it runs. The link is clean (`ComprisesValueAtConditionalArmRunLink`). Workaround: bind `self` at the listed type first, `r: R = self`, and write `r` in the arm. |

| NEW-K-3 | a compiled default body of a trait with a self-type parameter that calls a method on a value of that parameter dies at load, `ClassCircularityError`, where the object lists the trait first: `tagOf(other: S) = other.tag` in `trait Shape[\S extends Shape[\S\]\]`, for `object Pt extends Shape[\Pt\]` | NEGATIVE-BOUNDED | implementation gap (runtime) | `basic/traits.tex`, "Trait Declarations" | `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/XXXSelfTypeParameterReceiverRun.test` | climb batch 31 rung K | siblings: 695. 'ClassCircularityError: …$Pt', under `Class.forName` in `runtimeSystem/MethodInstantiater.java:269`, which loads the static argument's class to choose the call's opcode while that class's parent, the trait's instance, is expanded. Row 695's notes held it (`pick(self, other: S): S`); it stands on the base and after rung K. A body that does not call on the value runs; so does the trait bounded by another trait and listed second. The link is clean (`SelfTypeParameterReceiverRunLink`). Walk runs it. Workaround: declare the method in the object. |

| NEW-K-4 | on the compiled path an assignment from outside an object to its `var` field, of a value whose static type is a strict subtype of the field's type, dies at run time, `NoSuchMethodError`: `c.t := High` for `object Cell(var t: T)` and `object High extends T`; the checker accepts it and walk runs it | NEGATIVE-VERIFIED | implementation gap (codegen) | `basic/expressions/bindings.tex`, "Assignments" | `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/XXXVarFieldAssignedSubtypeRun.test` | climb batch 31 rung K | siblings: 397, 991. 'NoSuchMethodError: FVoid …$Cell.t(…$High)': the setter's call names the value's static type, not the field's. On the base and after rung K. The same for `c.r := self` in `trait Q comprises { R }` and `object Cell(var r: R)`: '…$Cell.r(…$Q)'; once the call names the field's type, that value needs the cast of `CodeGen.castToTypeBelow`. A value of the field's own type runs. The link is clean (`VarFieldAssignedSubtypeRunLink`). Workaround: bind the value at the field's type first, `h: T = High`, or assign in a method of the object. |

Rows NEW-K-3 and NEW-K-4 are the skeptic's; each has a run-time pair of expected-failure tests, and neither defect is changed by this rung (SKEPTIC.md).

`Specification/appendices/changes.tex:4437` cites NEW-K-1 by that placeholder; the gather puts the number in.

## Specification

`Specification/appendices/changes.tex:4431-4437`, the Effect of the self-type entry: the sentence on row 695 now says that the default body runs, and names the closure's departure (NEW-K-1). Not built here.

## Handover

Rung K landed on `wip/rung-comprises-cast` (`34fb6364d6`, `3139c8db39`): rows 991 and 695 close; two new expected failures, a closure's returned `self` and a conditional's arm (NEW-K-1, NEW-K-2), each one line in `forFnExpr`/`forLetFn` or `forIf` for a later rung; the count of the one library's methods that the verifier refuses still waits for a program compiled against the one library.

## Revival change

**The change.** The team's code generator emitted no cast where the checker reads `self` as more than its trait: `evalArg`'s single-argument branch evaluated the argument and cast nothing, and a method's body was returned as it stood (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java`, `evalArg` and `generateActualMethodCode` at the team's last commit). The specification gives `self` the type of its trait met with the types its `comprises` clause lists, or with its self-type parameter (`Specification/basic/expressions/var-ref.tex:64-76`), and the compiled checker accepts `den(self)` for `den(r: R)` in `trait Q comprises { R }`, and `twin(self): S = self` in `trait Shape[\S extends Shape[\S\]\]`. The compiled program then failed the JVM's verification when the trait's class loaded: 'VerifyError: Bad type on operand stack ... Type Q is not assignable to R', 'VerifyError: Bad return type'. The tree now casts a value that has self's type to a declared type strictly below its trait, at a single argument of a function, a method or a constructor, at a typed binding, at an assignment and at a method's returned value, also where the value is a typecase whose arms are each `self`: `compiler_tests/ComprisesValueAtListedTypeCompiled` and `compiler_tests/SelfTypeReturnSelfRun` run. Two places still fail and are written around by binding `self` at the listed type first, `r: R = self`: a function expression or a local function that returns `self` so (`compiler_tests/XXXComprisesValueFromClosureRun`), and a conditional with `self` in one arm and a listed value in the other (`compiler_tests/XXXComprisesValueAtConditionalArmRun`). A trait that lists a type at a `where`-clause variable gets no cast, and a call that opens its value to the variable still fails (`compiler_tests/XXXNatOpenRun`). A variable declared at the trait, other than `self`, does not stand at a listed type: the checker refuses it. A `typecase` on `self` narrows only through a binder, `c: Disc => f(c)`.

**Provenance.** Rows 991 and 695 of the gap ledger; P-60 and P-146; fork K1 of the batch record, built narrower than its default (REPORT.md, decision 1); climb batch 31, rung K.

The interpreter has no static types: it runs the bodies as before, and loads a
declaration that the paragraph refuses (row~893 of the revival's gap ledger).
The code generator converts \KWD{self} to the type of the instance where a default
body returns it as the self parameter, passes it as a single argument, binds it or
assigns it at that type, so a compiled program that runs such a body with the
parameter at an object type runs.
A function expression or a local function that returns \KWD{self} as the self
parameter still fails the JVM's verification when its class is loaded
(row~1050 of the revival's gap ledger).
\item[Original text] \nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/var-ref.tex},
101:- F-225 **In a self-typed trait with no `comprises` clause, or one that lists only `...`, the compiled checker types `self` in the method bodies as `C[\X\] & X`, the trait met with the implementing type, read from the trait's F-bound; the methods' signatures keep `self` at the plain trait type `C[\X\]`, save in the overloading check's exclusion test (F-277), and the checker refuses an extender at another type.** It builds P-146. A self-typed trait is a trait `C[\X\]` whose parameter `X` extends `C[\X\]`. The checker also takes a parameter bounded by a self-typed trait that the trait extends at that parameter, as the team's `Containment` mixins are: a default of the coordinator's. In a trait whose `comprises` clause lists types, `self` is instead the trait met with the union of those types, and the exclusion test reads its signatures plain. For example, `object Bad extends Integral[\ZZ32\]` is refused, since `Bad` is not a `ZZ32`. The rule accepts every self-typed body of the library but `Integral`'s `numerator`, which each integer type declares instead (P-146). Walk has no such rule and loads what it refuses. A compiled default body that returns `self` dies at class load with a `VerifyError` when the trait's self-type parameter is an object type, as in `object Pt(…) extends Shape[\Pt\]`: an open defect (row 695). The rule refuses, rightly, a team declaration, `PureList`'s `List` (row 355); the demo `trips.fss`'s `generator`, which it refused, extends `StandardTotalOrder[\generator\]` since its repair (row 710; `ProjectFortress/demos/trips.fss:96`). The compiler's prelude writes the self type instead as `comprises T` on `StandardTotalOrder` and `Equality` (`Library/CompilerAlgebra.fsi:16`, `:24`; on `StandardTotalOrder` since Steele's `655e65d53`, 2012-06-05, and `59fdeff62`, 2012-06-06, which took its F-bound away), and that spelling does not bind the one library, since Naden's last text puts the self-type idiom in bounds only, not as a first-class type (`Papers/Types/journal/justificationOfRTR.tex:626-630`), and Steele's own message on `655e65d53` gives the self type as the trait met with the `comprises` clause, which this rule reads from the F-bound. Gated by `compiler_tests/SelfType*` and `XXXSelfType*`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-self-type/REPORT.md` sections 1, 2, 4 and 7; `compile-ladder/rung-self-type-exclusion/REPORT.md` section 1.

## Building it

To check your LaTeX, build the specification in a built tree, after the setup lines. It takes about 90 s, so start it detached (`session.md`, "Long commands"):

    nohup bash -c '( cd Specification/fortress && ./ant genSource && ./ant tex ) > tmp/spec.txt 2>&1; echo EXIT=$? >> tmp/spec.txt' >/dev/null 2>&1 &

- Both commands must end in `BUILD SUCCESSFUL`, and `grep -c 'LaTeX Warning: Reference\|LaTeX Warning: Label .* multiply defined\|LaTeX Warning: There were multiply-defined labels\|^! Undefined control sequence' Specification/fortress/fortress.log` must print 0.
- If `pdflatex` is missing, install the packages of the `PKGS` line of `explorations/experiment/setup.sh` with `apt-get update -qq && apt-get install -y`.
- The build writes only ignored files, its log among them, which can reach 400 MB. Remove them afterwards: `git clean -fXq -- Specification`.
- Update `Specification/fortress.pdf` only if your brief asks for it: copy `Specification/fortress/fortress.pdf` over it.

## The self-return at an object type

My first shape of step 1's test had `object Late(x: ZZ32) extends { Named, Tord[\Late\] }`. With the duplicate gone, the run died while `Tord⟦Late⟧`'s class loaded:

    Caused by: java.lang.VerifyError: Bad return type
      Location: ...$\=Tord?...\%Late?$DefaultTraitMethods.mx?0(...)
      Reason: Type 'java/lang/Object' (current frame, stack[0]) is not assignable to 'TraitOwnMethodBesideInheritedCompiled$Late' (from method signature)

`Tord`'s `mx(self, other: T): T = if lt(other, self) then self else other` returns `self` as `T`: row 695, which rung K repairs. At a trait instance (`Z`, `Y`) the JVM's verifier passes it, since it does not check assignment to an interface. So I made `Late` a trait with an object below it, and took the object case, an object whose second trait declares a method again, into two traits whose bodies do not return `self` (`Shown`, `Marked`, `Leaf`). The library's own `MAX` in `StandardTotalOrder` has `Tord`'s body, so after this rung an object that extends such a trait directly still waits for rung K.

(* A generic trait that gives a body to a method which it also inherits with a body, through an extended trait that is not its first, runs its own body, as does a type below it that declares the method again (traits.tex, section "Method Declarations"). *)
component TraitOwnMethodBesideInheritedCompiled
export Executable

trait Eqq[\T extends Eqq[\T\]\]
    eqv(self, other: T): Boolean = true
end
trait Pord[\T extends Pord[\T\]\] extends { Eqq[\T\] }
    lt(self, other: T): Boolean = (cmpx(self, other) = -1)
    cmpx(self, other: T): ZZ32 = if lt(self, other) then -1 elif lt(other, self) then 1 else 0 end
    eqv(self, other: T): Boolean = (cmpx(self, other) = 0)
end
trait Mmx[\T extends Mmx[\T\]\]
    mnmx(self, other: T): (T, T)
    mx(self, other: T): T = do (a, r) = mnmx(self, other); r end
    opr UPPER(self, other: T): String = "Mmx"
    whose(): String = "Mmx"
end
trait Tord[\T extends Tord[\T\]\] extends { Pord[\T\], Mmx[\T\] }
    cmpx(self, other: T): ZZ32 = if lt(self, other) then -1 elif lt(other, self) then 1 else 0 end
    mx(self, other: T): T = if lt(other, self) then self else other end
    mnmx(self, other: T): (T, T) = if lt(other, self) then (other, self) else (self, other) end
    opr UPPER(self, other: T): String = "Tord"
    whose(): String = "Tord"
end
trait Z extends { Tord[\Z\] }
    getter v(): ZZ32
    lt(self, other: Z): Boolean = self.v < other.v
    eqv(self, other: Z): Boolean = self.v = other.v
    cmpx(self, other: Z): ZZ32 = if lt(self, other) then -1 elif lt(other, self) then 1 else 0 end
    mnmx(self, other: Z): (Z, Z) = if lt(other, self) then (other, self) else (self, other) end
    opr UPPER(self, other: Z): String = "Z"
    whose(): String = "Z"
end
object Zint(x: ZZ32) extends Z
    getter v(): ZZ32 = x
end
trait Y extends { Tord[\Y\] }
    getter w(): ZZ32
    lt(self, other: Y): Boolean = self.w < other.w
